To Reproduce
When I am training the deep-learning network, I get the following RuntimeError :
RuntimeError: shmem_size <= sharedMemPerBlock INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/opt/conda/conda-bld/pytorch_1603729128610/work/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/AdaptiveAveragePooling.cu":669, please report a bug to PyTorch.

Note that I use quite a lot of nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d in my network.

nodes.bodyText:
As we know, we can register forward hooks for nn.Module instances. But there are functional operations like nn.functional.interpolate(),  or torch.cat(), or even an implicit callable like <built-in function add>  for element-wise summation of tensor_a and tensor_b like this:
tensor_c = tensor_a + tensor_b  # There is a <built-in function add>  here
Can we use hooks for these functional calls?
nodes.title: Can we register forward hooks for functional calls?

🚀 Feature
#68155 is adding preliminary support for auto wrapping in FSDP API, but needs some follow up work. In particular, it relies on ConfigAutoWrap.recursive_wrap to reuse existing checked in code, but we should clean this up and only maintain the needed portion of wrap.py: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/_fsdp/wrap.py and remove the dependency on ConfigAutoWrap.
cc @zhaojuanmao @mrshenli @rohan-varma

Example script: https://gist.github.com/nkreeger/de850a106c394ebbd213fd29ed3955ba
This script throws an error because the calls to the Proxy constructor in the inner loop each instantiate a new GraphAppendingTracer. When these Proxys with different tracers are used together in an n-ary operator (e.g. binary operators like add), an exception is thrown because more than one tracer instance was found in the arguments. Modifying the script to instantiate a single GraphAppendingTracer and use that consistently throughout fixes the issue: https://gist.github.com/jamesr66a/d36bd887459e9089910120bb9a489ff5
We should update our examples and documentation to use this approach. We should also see if we can improve this API in some way to make it more obvious what the correct thing to do is.

This is a followup to #63781. The approach there has a few problems, namely that it was focused too narrowly on avoiding tests. While this might be good in the future (i.e. some codebases want to run a limited subset of tests and are OK with the increased revert risk), we need a more fundamental approach to dynamically controlling workflows that run on PRs.
Goal
Decrease time to signal (TTS) on PRs by running fewer jobs. Note that this is different from #63781, that RFC suggested doing less work within jobs (by limiting the tests that run, this is also how the old/dead TD we used to have worked).
Implementation
Both approaches use CIFlow to determine the jobs to run.
in-repo
We put the logic to decide if subsequent jobs should run in a file (say tools/determinator/main.py) that prints out a true/false at the end. Then we can skip other jobs based on this, similar to how we use needs: [ciflow_should_run] in workflows today. This is nice since the triggering logic isn't very complicated and can be defined by Python that lives in the repo. However, any changes to determination would require users to rebase (i.e. if we edit rules or there is a bug)
probot
We can put the logic to inspect PRs into probot and use that to decide what labels to add to PRs. We'd probably have to extends CIFlow to have a concept of exclusive labels (for a case like doc-only PRs, we want to not run the default jobs and only run a doc build + preview workflow). Probot could then add labels based on PR content similar to how it does now and we edit the workflows to conditionally execute based on these labels.

class _LowerTriangular(Constraint):

🐛 Bug
In multi-node training, when one or more elastic agents gets killed with a SIGINT, SIGTERM, (and additionally SIGHUP, and SIGQUIT on windows), scale down does not work even when the surviving agents are compliant with the min - max sizes.
This is because of two things:


When creating the trainer child processes, the agent will self register a termination handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM (and on windows adds in SIGHUP and SIGQUIT as well) that will raise a SignalException (
  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/elastic/multiprocessing/api.py
    
    
         Line 233
      in
      cd51d2a
    
  
  
    

        
          
           signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, _terminate_process_handler) 
        
    
  

)


In launcher/api.py#launch_agent() (
  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/launcher/api.py
    
    
         Line 274
      in
      cd51d2a
    
  
  
    

        
          
           rdzv_handler.shutdown() 
        
    
  

), agent.run() is wrapped in a try-catch-finally block where the finally block calls rdzv_handler.shutdown() on an exception.


The issue with 1) and 2) combined is that when the agent dies with a signal, it produces a python exception (which is not the norm other than SIGINT) and hence rdzv_handler.shutdown() is invoked in the finally block. On the other hand rdzv_handler.shutdown() should ONLY be called during an orderly shutdown (e.g. when the job has finished successfully or it has exhuasted the max_restarts), and SHOULD NOT be called on premature agent failures.
When the shutdown() method on rendezvous is called, this (by design) closes the current rendezvous permanently. Hence disallowing any more scaling events to take place where any agent attempting to join the training job will fail with a RendezvousClosedException.
To Fix
NOTE: Removing termination handlers for SIGTERM, SIGINT IS NOT A VIABLE FIX since this logic was specifically added to ensure (in an os independent way) that agents do not leave orphaned child workers when the agent dies prematurely
What we probably need to do is to catch the SignalException explicitly in 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/launcher/api.py
    
    
         Line 265
      in
      cd51d2a
    
  
  
    

        
          
           except ChildFailedError: 
        
    
  

 and NOT call rdzv_handler.shutdown() in this case.

         Line 810
      in
      cd51d2a
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def double_agent_fault_tolerance(self): 
        
    
  

) which didn't catch this bug since the bug is due to a cross module combination between a newly introduced SignalException in the agent and the existing try-catch-finally block in the launcher/api.py. When we fix this, we should also introduce a unittest specifically testing this cross module dependency.

This is a small issue: pytorch tests have warnings when run on master (hash: 82f7f8d).
While this is clearly not a glaring issue, I think that tests ought not to produce warnings when running. It makes it harder for developers to see whether or not that is produced by their work.
Secondly, I think it is generally worth following the paradigms we expect to code with when we write tests.
Does this seem reasonable?
To Reproduce

python test/test_optim.py

In PyTorch 1.1.0 and later, you should call them in the opposite order: `optimizer.step()` before `lr_scheduler.step()`.  Failure to do this will result in PyTorch skipping the first value of the learning rate schedule. See more details at https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/optim.html#how-to-adjust-learning-rate
 warnings.warn("Detected call of `lr_scheduler.step()` before `optimizer.step()`. "

s illegal value. Most certainly there is a bug in the implementation calling the backend library."

To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Install PyTorch 1.10.0 from sources, building against OpenBLAS 0.3.15
Run python run_test.py -i test_linalg.TestLinalgCPU -v to run the relevant part of the test suite
(alternative): instead of running the test from the test suite, simply do

import torch
a = torch.full((3, 3), float('nan'), dtype=torch.float32, device='cpu')
torch.svd(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):

torch.svd(a)

           def is_avx512_vnni_supported():
